course: AP Psychology - Behaviour, Evidence and Explanation
attribution: Original scope and sequence authored for the Luminfest Learning Harness, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: The AP Psychology framework: the vocabulary of evidence, biological bases of behaviour, cognition, development and learning, social psychology and personality, and mental and physical health.

concepts.title: Structuralism and introspection
concepts.summary: Wundt and Titchener tried to break conscious experience into its elements, training observers to report what a stimulus felt like rather than what it was.

concepts.title: Functionalism
concepts.summary: James asked what consciousness is for rather than what it is made of, so mental processes were explained by their adaptive value.

concepts.title: Psychoanalytic perspective
concepts.summary: Freud located behaviour in unconscious conflict and early experience, which is why the same situation can produce anxiety the person cannot explain.

concepts.title: Behaviourist perspective
concepts.summary: Behaviourism studies only what can be observed, and explains it by the consequences that followed it rather than by inner states.

concepts.title: Humanistic perspective
concepts.summary: Rogers and Maslow argued that people are driven toward growth and self-direction, so a person is not reducible to drives or reinforcement.

concepts.title: Cognitive perspective
concepts.summary: The cognitive perspective explains behaviour through the mental processes between stimulus and response: attention, encoding, retrieval and decision.

concepts.title: Biological perspective
concepts.summary: The biological perspective explains behaviour through genes, brain structures, neurotransmitters and hormones.

concepts.title: Evolutionary perspective
concepts.summary: The evolutionary perspective asks which adaptive problem a trait solved, so a behaviour is explained by the survival or reproductive advantage it once carried.

concepts.title: Sociocultural perspective
concepts.summary: The sociocultural perspective explains behaviour through culture, norms and social situation, so the same act can mean different things in different groups.

concepts.title: Biopsychosocial approach
concepts.summary: A complete explanation combines biological, psychological and social levels rather than choosing one, because each level answers a different question about the same behaviour.

concepts.title: Hypothesis and operational definition
concepts.summary: A hypothesis is a testable prediction, and an operational definition states exactly how a variable will be measured so another researcher could repeat it.

concepts.title: Independent and dependent variables
concepts.summary: The independent variable is what the researcher manipulates; the dependent variable is what is measured as the outcome.

concepts.title: Confounding variables
concepts.summary: A confound is an unintended difference between conditions that could produce the effect instead of the manipulated variable.

concepts.title: Random assignment and random sampling
concepts.summary: Random sampling decides who is in the study; random assignment decides which condition each participant enters. Only assignment supports a causal claim.

concepts.title: Experimental and correlational designs
concepts.summary: An experiment manipulates a variable and can establish cause; a correlational study measures two variables as they occur and cannot.

concepts.title: Correlation coefficient
concepts.summary: A correlation coefficient runs from -1 to +1 and reports the strength and direction of a relationship; its size says nothing about causation.

concepts.title: Naturalistic observation and case study
concepts.summary: Naturalistic observation watches behaviour where it happens, and a case study examines one person in depth; both describe richly but neither controls variables.

concepts.title: Survey and self-report bias
concepts.summary: Surveys depend on what people say about themselves, so wording, social desirability and inaccurate self-knowledge all distort the data.

concepts.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional designs
concepts.summary: A longitudinal design follows one group over time and a cross-sectional design compares age groups at one moment; cohort differences are the price of the faster design.

concepts.title: Reliability and validity
concepts.summary: Reliability is consistency of measurement and validity is whether the measure actually captures the construct, so a test can be reliable without being valid.

concepts.title: Replication and publication bias
concepts.summary: A finding counts when independent researchers reproduce it; studies that fail to replicate tend to go unpublished, which inflates the published literature.

concepts.title: Measures of central tendency
concepts.summary: Mean, median and mode summarise a distribution differently, and the mean is the one an outlier drags away from the centre.

concepts.title: Variation and standard deviation
concepts.summary: Two groups can share a mean and differ completely in spread, which is why standard deviation is reported beside the average.

concepts.title: Normal distribution and percentile rank
concepts.summary: In a normal distribution most scores cluster near the mean and fall away symmetrically, so a percentile describes position rather than percentage correct.

concepts.title: Inferential statistics and significance
concepts.summary: A significance test estimates how often a difference this large would appear by chance alone; a small p-value is evidence against chance, not proof of importance.

concepts.title: Effect size
concepts.summary: Effect size reports how large a difference is in standardised units, which is why a statistically significant result can still be trivial.

concepts.title: Informed consent and debriefing
concepts.summary: Participants must agree to take part knowing the risks, and must be told the true purpose afterwards, especially when deception was used.

concepts.title: Confidentiality and protection from harm
concepts.summary: Data must be kept private and participants must leave the study no worse than they arrived, which is the standard an ethics board applies.

concepts.title: Placebo and double-blind procedure
concepts.summary: A placebo control separates the effect of expecting improvement from the effect of the treatment, and blinding keeps the experimenter from communicating that expectation.

concepts.title: Experimenter and demand characteristics
concepts.summary: Cues in a study tell participants what is expected of them, so behaviour can reflect the hypothesis rather than the manipulation.

concepts.title: Behaviour genetics and twin studies
concepts.summary: Comparing identical and fraternal twins separates the contribution of shared genes from shared environment, because both kinds of twin share a home but only one kind shares all its genes.

concepts.title: Heritability
concepts.summary: Heritability estimates how much of the variation in a group is explained by genetic differences; it is a property of a population, not a fixed share of one person.

concepts.title: Gene-environment interaction
concepts.summary: Genes set a range of possible outcomes and environment decides where inside that range a person lands, so the same genotype can develop differently.

concepts.title: Epigenetics
concepts.summary: Experience can switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence, which is how stress or diet in one generation can shape expression in the next.

concepts.title: Neuron structure
concepts.summary: A neuron receives at dendrites, integrates at the cell body and transmits down the axon to terminals, which is why damage to different parts produces different deficits.

concepts.title: Action potential
concepts.summary: A neuron fires all-or-none when excitation passes threshold, so intensity is coded by firing rate rather than by a bigger impulse.

concepts.title: Neurotransmitters
concepts.summary: Neurotransmitters cross the synapse and bind to receptors, turning the signal into excitation or inhibition in the next cell.

concepts.title: Agonists and antagonists
concepts.summary: An agonist mimics or strengthens a neurotransmitter and an antagonist blocks it, which is how most psychiatric drugs change behaviour.

concepts.title: Reuptake and synaptic plasticity
concepts.summary: Reuptake clears transmitter from the gap, and repeated signalling strengthens or weakens the synapse, which is the cellular basis of learning.

concepts.title: Central and peripheral nervous system
concepts.summary: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral system carries sensory input in and motor commands out.

concepts.title: Somatic and autonomic nervous system
concepts.summary: The somatic division controls voluntary movement and the autonomic division runs involuntary functions, which is why arousal happens without a decision.

concepts.title: Sympathetic and parasympathetic division
concepts.summary: The sympathetic division mobilises the body for threat and the parasympathetic division restores and conserves, so they pull against each other.

concepts.title: Endocrine system and hormones
concepts.summary: Glands release hormones into the blood, so their effects are slower and longer-lasting than neural signals.

concepts.title: Brainstem and cerebellum
concepts.summary: The brainstem sustains automatic survival functions and the cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, which is why damage shows up as clumsiness rather than as lost knowledge.

concepts.title: Limbic system
concepts.summary: The amygdala tags emotional significance, the hippocampus forms new memories and the hypothalamus regulates drives, so emotion, memory and motivation share one circuit.

concepts.title: Cerebral cortex and lobes
concepts.summary: The occipital lobe processes vision, the temporal lobe hearing and language, the parietal lobe touch and spatial location, and the frontal lobe movement, planning and inhibition.

concepts.title: Hemispheric specialisation and split brain
concepts.summary: The hemispheres specialise, and when the connecting fibres are cut each half behaves as though it did not know what the other perceived.

concepts.title: Neuroplasticity
concepts.summary: The brain reorganises its connections with experience, which is why recovery after injury and skill learning are possible at all.

concepts.title: Brain imaging techniques
concepts.summary: EEG records electrical activity quickly, MRI and CT show structure, and PET and fMRI show activity, so each technique answers a different question.

concepts.title: Circadian rhythm
concepts.summary: An internal clock of roughly twenty-four hours regulates alertness and body temperature, and light is what resets it.

concepts.title: Sleep stages
concepts.summary: Sleep cycles through light, deep and REM stages, and the EEG signature changes with each because brain activity differs.

concepts.title: Sleep disorders
concepts.summary: Insomnia, narcolepsy and sleep apnoea are distinguished by what fails - falling asleep, staying awake, or breathing - not by how tired the person feels.

concepts.title: Theories of dreaming
concepts.summary: Freudian, activation-synthesis and cognitive views disagree about whether dreams express hidden conflict, assemble random activity into a story, or consolidate memory.

concepts.title: Sensation and perception
concepts.summary: Sensation is the detection of a stimulus and perception is its interpretation, so the same physical input can yield different experience.

concepts.title: Transduction and thresholds
concepts.summary: Transduction converts one form of energy into neural signals, and the absolute and difference thresholds mark the weakest detectable stimulus and the smallest detectable change.

concepts.title: Signal detection and sensory adaptation
concepts.summary: Detection depends on both sensitivity and response bias, and adaptation means a constant stimulus fades from awareness.

concepts.title: Vision: rods, cones and the retina
concepts.summary: Rods work in dim light without colour and cones give colour and detail, so night vision is poor in colour and colour vision is poor in the dark.

concepts.title: Audition: pitch and localisation
concepts.summary: Place and frequency coding together explain pitch, and timing and loudness differences between the ears explain where a sound comes from.

concepts.title: Touch, pain and the body senses
concepts.summary: Nociceptors signal tissue damage, gate control explains why attention changes pain, and the vestibular and kinesthetic senses report balance and limb position.

concepts.title: Bottom-up and top-down processing
concepts.summary: Bottom-up processing builds a percept from features and top-down processing applies expectation, which is why a blurry word becomes readable in context.

concepts.title: Perceptual constancy
concepts.summary: Size, shape and colour stay stable across changing retinal images, so we see a door as rectangular while its image is a trapezoid.

concepts.title: Gestalt principles of grouping
concepts.summary: Proximity, similarity, continuity and closure describe how elements are grouped into wholes, because perception organises rather than records.

concepts.title: Depth perception and binocular cues
concepts.summary: Convergence and retinal disparity use two eyes, and relative size, interposition and linear perspective work with one, which is why depth survives closing an eye.

concepts.title: Selective and divided attention
concepts.summary: Selective attention filters input by relevance and divided attention splits capacity, which is why two demanding tasks degrade together.

concepts.title: Perceptual set and context
concepts.summary: Expectation, context and culture bias what is perceived, so the same ambiguous figure resolves differently for different observers.

concepts.title: Three-stage model of memory
concepts.summary: Sensory memory holds a trace briefly, working memory holds a few items while they are used, and long-term memory stores effectively without limit.

concepts.title: Encoding and levels of processing
concepts.summary: Deep, meaning-based encoding produces better retention than shallow structural encoding, which is why elaborating beats rereading.

concepts.title: Chunking and working-memory capacity
concepts.summary: Working memory holds about four chunks, and grouping items into larger units raises the amount carried without raising the capacity.

concepts.title: Retrieval: recall and recognition
concepts.summary: Recall reproduces information and recognition identifies it, and recognition is usually easier because the cue is present.

concepts.title: Forgetting: decay and interference
concepts.summary: Traces fade with disuse and similar material interferes, with proactive interference blocking new learning and retroactive interference blocking old.

concepts.title: Reconstructive memory and the misinformation effect
concepts.summary: Memory is rebuilt at retrieval, so misleading post-event information can be incorporated as though it had been witnessed.

concepts.title: Spacing, testing and the serial position effect
concepts.summary: Distributed practice and retrieval practice beat massed rereading, and the primacy and recency effects show that position in a list changes what is remembered.

concepts.title: Concepts and prototypes
concepts.summary: A concept groups similar things and a prototype is the best example of the category, so categorisation is graded rather than all-or-nothing.

concepts.title: Algorithms and heuristics
concepts.summary: An algorithm guarantees a solution by trying every option and a heuristic trades certainty for speed, which is why heuristics produce predictable errors.

concepts.title: Availability and representativeness heuristics
concepts.summary: The availability heuristic judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind and the representativeness heuristic judges it by resemblance to a stereotype.

concepts.title: Confirmation bias and belief perseverance
concepts.summary: People seek evidence that fits a existing belief and discount what contradicts it, so a wrong belief can survive disconfirming data.

concepts.title: Framing and loss aversion
concepts.summary: The same choice framed as a gain or a loss produces different decisions, because losses weigh more than equivalent gains.

concepts.title: Language structure and development
concepts.summary: Phonemes, morphemes, syntax and semantics are separate levels, and children acquire them in a predictable order without explicit instruction.

concepts.title: Linguistic relativity
concepts.summary: Language shapes the categories available for thought, so a distinction encoded in words is easier to notice and remember.

concepts.title: Intelligence as psychometric g
concepts.summary: Scores on diverse mental tests correlate, which supports a general factor behind performance while leaving room for specific abilities.

concepts.title: Standardisation, reliability and validity of tests
concepts.summary: A test is standardised on a norm group, and its scores are only interpretable if it measures consistently and predicts what it claims to predict.

concepts.title: Stereotype threat and test bias
concepts.summary: Awareness of a negative stereotype about one group can depress performance, so a group difference is not evidence about ability.
prerequisites: Standardisation, reliability and validity of tests

concepts.title: Creativity and divergent thinking
concepts.summary: Creativity combines expertise, imaginative thinking skills and a venturesome personality, so it is a profile rather than a single score.

concepts.title: Prenatal development and teratogens
concepts.summary: Development proceeds through germinal, embryonic and fetal stages, and a teratogen is any agent that damages the developing organism during a critical period.

concepts.title: Piaget stages of cognitive development
concepts.summary: Children move from sensorimotor action to preoperational symbolism, then concrete operations, then formal operations, with each stage defined by what the child can now do that it could not before.

concepts.title: Assimilation and accommodation
concepts.summary: Assimilation fits new experience into an existing schema and accommodation changes the schema, and the tension between them drives stage change.

concepts.title: Object permanence and conservation
concepts.summary: Object permanence is knowing a thing continues to exist unseen and conservation is knowing quantity survives a change of appearance; both fail in the young child and mark stage boundaries.

concepts.title: Vygotsky and the zone of proximal development
concepts.summary: Learning is social first, and the zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and with support, which is what scaffolding targets.

concepts.title: Attachment and the strange situation
concepts.summary: Attachment forms in the first year, and Ainsworth classified secure, avoidant and ambivalent patterns by how an infant reacts to separation and reunion.

concepts.title: Parenting styles
concepts.summary: Authoritative parenting, high in warmth and demand, is associated with the best outcomes, while authoritarian, permissive and neglectful styles are not.

concepts.title: Erikson psychosocial stages
concepts.summary: Each stage poses a crisis between two outcomes, and resolution shapes the next stage, which is why identity work dominates adolescence.

concepts.title: Kohlberg moral development
concepts.summary: Moral reasoning moves from consequences, to social approval and law, to abstract principle, and the stage is about the reason given rather than the choice made.

concepts.title: Adolescent brain and identity
concepts.summary: The limbic system matures before the prefrontal cortex, so sensation seeking peaks before impulse control catches up.

concepts.title: Gender and sexual orientation development
concepts.summary: Gender identity, expression and orientation develop from interacting biological, cognitive and social influences rather than one cause.

concepts.title: Ageing and cognitive change
concepts.summary: Fluid abilities decline earlier than crystallised ones, so vocabulary can hold while processing speed falls.

concepts.title: Classical conditioning
concepts.summary: A neutral stimulus paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus comes to elicit the response alone, which is how a physiological reaction gets attached to a new cue.

concepts.title: Acquisition, extinction and spontaneous recovery
concepts.summary: Acquisition builds the association, extinction weakens it when the pairing stops, and spontaneous recovery shows the original learning was suppressed rather than erased.

concepts.title: Generalisation and discrimination
concepts.summary: A response generalises to stimuli similar to the conditioned one and discrimination narrows it to the one that predicts the outcome.

concepts.title: Operant conditioning
concepts.summary: Behaviour is shaped by its consequences: reinforcement raises the probability of a response and punishment lowers it.

concepts.title: Positive and negative reinforcement
concepts.summary: Both reinforcement types increase behaviour; positive adds a consequence and negative removes one, which is why negative reinforcement is not punishment.

concepts.title: Schedules of reinforcement
concepts.summary: Ratio schedules count responses and interval schedules count time, and variable schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones.

concepts.title: Observational learning
concepts.summary: Bandura showed that behaviour is acquired by watching a model and its consequences, so learning can occur without the learner being reinforced.

concepts.title: Latent learning and cognitive maps
concepts.summary: Learning can occur without performance and without reward, appearing only when an incentive makes it useful.

concepts.title: Biological constraints on conditioning
concepts.summary: Some associations form far more easily than others, so preparedness limits what can be conditioned in a species.

concepts.title: Attribution theory and the fundamental attribution error
concepts.summary: People explain behaviour by disposition or situation, and the fundamental attribution error is over-weighting disposition when judging others.

concepts.title: Attitudes and cognitive dissonance
concepts.summary: An attitude is an evaluation that guides behaviour, and dissonance is the discomfort of holding inconsistent cognitions, usually resolved by changing the attitude.

concepts.title: Conformity and normative influence
concepts.summary: Asch showed that people yield to a unanimous wrong majority, because fitting in and being right are separate pressures.

concepts.title: Obedience to authority
concepts.summary: Milgram showed that ordinary people follow an authority instruction that harms another person when the situation makes each step small and the authority takes responsibility.

concepts.title: Group influence: facilitation, loafing and polarisation
concepts.summary: Presence of others improves simple performance and impairs complex performance, individual effort drops when it cannot be identified, and discussion pushes a group toward a more extreme position.

concepts.title: Groupthink and deindividuation
concepts.summary: Groupthink suppresses dissent in the interest of harmony and deindividuation reduces self-awareness in a crowd, so both loosen restraint.
prerequisites: Group influence: facilitation, loafing and polarisation

concepts.title: Prejudice, stereotypes and discrimination
concepts.summary: A stereotype is a belief about a group, prejudice is an attitude toward it, and discrimination is behaviour; the three can occur separately.

concepts.title: Bystander effect and altruism
concepts.summary: Helping drops as the number of witnesses rises, because responsibility is diffused and each person reads the others as not alarmed.

concepts.title: Attraction and interpersonal factors
concepts.summary: Proximity, physical attractiveness, similarity and reciprocity of liking predict attraction better than the idea of opposites attracting.

concepts.title: Psychodynamic structure: id, ego and superego
concepts.summary: The id seeks immediate gratification, the superego enforces internalised rules, and the ego negotiates between them and reality.

concepts.title: Defence mechanisms
concepts.summary: The ego reduces anxiety by distorting reality - repression, projection, displacement, rationalisation - which protects the self at the cost of accuracy.
prerequisites: Psychodynamic structure: id, ego and superego

concepts.title: Humanistic self-concept
concepts.summary: Rogers held that growth requires unconditional positive regard, and that a gap between the real and ideal self produces incongruence.

concepts.title: Trait theory and the Big Five
concepts.summary: Trait models describe stable, continuous differences; the Big Five - openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism - summarise them with better predictive validity than type labels.

concepts.title: Social-cognitive theory and locus of control
concepts.summary: Behaviour results from the interaction of person, behaviour and environment, and locus of control is the belief that outcomes depend on one's own actions or on outside forces.

concepts.title: Projective and objective personality tests
concepts.summary: Projective tests interpret ambiguous stimuli and objective tests score fixed items; the second is far more reliable, whatever the first claims to reveal.
prerequisites: Trait theory and the Big Five

concepts.title: Drive-reduction and arousal theory
concepts.summary: Drive-reduction explains behaviour as restoring balance, and arousal theory explains it as seeking an optimal level of stimulation.

concepts.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
concepts.summary: Intrinsic motivation comes from the activity itself and extrinsic from its consequences, and heavy external reward can undercut the first.

concepts.title: Maslow hierarchy of needs
concepts.summary: Needs are arranged from physiological to self-actualisation, and lower needs dominate attention until they are met.

concepts.title: Theories of emotion
concepts.summary: James-Lange says the body reaction comes first, Cannon-Bard says body and feeling occur together, and Schachter-Singer says arousal plus a cognitive label produces the emotion.

concepts.title: Stress and the general adaptation syndrome
concepts.summary: Selye described alarm, resistance and exhaustion, which is why prolonged stress damages health rather than merely feeling unpleasant.

concepts.title: Appraisal and coping
concepts.summary: Lazarus held that stress depends on whether an event is appraised as threatening and whether resources are judged sufficient, so coping follows appraisal.

concepts.title: Health psychology and behaviour
concepts.summary: Health psychology links behaviour - sleep, exercise, smoking, adherence - to physical outcomes, because most chronic disease has a behavioural component.

concepts.title: Positive psychology and well-being
concepts.summary: Positive psychology studies what makes life go well rather than only what goes wrong, measuring engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment alongside pleasant feeling.

concepts.title: Resilience and social support
concepts.summary: Resilience is the capacity to recover after adversity, and social support is one of the strongest predictors of recovery.

concepts.title: Classifying disorder: the DSM and diagnosis
concepts.summary: A classification system names clusters of symptoms so clinicians agree on what they are treating; a diagnosis describes a pattern and is not a statement about the person.

concepts.title: Diathesis-stress model
concepts.summary: Disorder appears when a vulnerability meets a stressor, which is why the same stressor harms one person and not another.
prerequisites: Classifying disorder: the DSM and diagnosis

concepts.title: Anxiety disorders
concepts.summary: Generalised anxiety, panic disorder, phobia and social anxiety share excessive fear but differ in what triggers it and how it is avoided.

concepts.title: Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders
concepts.summary: Obsessions are intrusive thoughts and compulsions are repeated acts that reduce the distress, so the compulsion is maintained by relief rather than by pleasure.

concepts.title: Depressive and bipolar disorders
concepts.summary: Major depression is a sustained low mood or loss of interest, and bipolar disorder adds episodes of elevated mood, which is why the two are treated differently.

concepts.title: Schizophrenia spectrum
concepts.summary: Positive symptoms add experience - hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech - and negative symptoms subtract it, such as flat affect and withdrawal.

concepts.title: Dissociative and somatic symptom disorders
concepts.summary: Dissociative disorders involve disruption of identity or memory and somatic symptom disorders involve bodily complaints without a matching medical explanation.

concepts.title: Neurodevelopmental and personality disorders
concepts.summary: Neurodevelopmental disorders appear early and affect development, while personality disorders are enduring patterns of relating that are rigid and cause impairment.

concepts.title: Psychodynamic and humanistic therapy
concepts.summary: Psychodynamic therapy works on insight into unconscious patterns and humanistic therapy on self-acceptance and growth, so both aim at understanding rather than at a specific behaviour.

concepts.title: Cognitive-behavioural therapy
concepts.summary: CBT changes the thoughts and behaviours that maintain a problem, and it has the strongest evidence base of the talking therapies for anxiety and depression.

concepts.title: Behavioural therapy and exposure
concepts.summary: Exposure works by preventing the avoidance that keeps a fear alive, so the extinction is experienced rather than argued.

concepts.title: Biomedical treatments
concepts.summary: Psychopharmacology changes neurotransmitter signalling - SSRIs for depression, antipsychotics for psychosis, lithium for bipolar - and medication and therapy are often combined.

concepts.title: Evaluating treatment effectiveness
concepts.summary: Improvement must be compared with no treatment and with placebo, because many conditions improve on their own and expectation alone produces change.
